> an enclosure for the pcbBedLift is a 3D-printed laptop stand for 13-14" laptops that folds flat and works on a lap or a mattress. The tilted, vented tray lets heat escape. A foam-cushioned front edge and wide slip-on foot boots keep it from digging into a lap or sinking into bedding. It prints on a standard 220 mm bed in PETG as a two-piece tray joined by bow-tie keys, with hinged legs held by M4 bolts. The whole design is parametric, so the tilt, tray size and fit can be changed from a short Python script. The parts cost about $61 including estimated shipping.

## Design

### 2026-10-17 – ## What I did this session

**6h**

## What I did this session

I designed **BedLift**, a foldable, vented laptop stand for 13-14" laptops that works on a lap or a mattress, and prepared everything needed to submit it: CAD files, printable STLs, a BOM and a README. I worked with Claude (an AI assistant) to generate the CAD as a parametric Python/CadQuery script, then checked, rendered and documented the results myself.

### Design
- Started from a sample STEP file, brainstormed ideas, and chose a **foldable laptop stand with vent cutouts**. Then I changed the brief to "usable in bed".
- Final design: **300 × 200 × 10 mm tray tilted 20°**, 36 vent slots, an 8 mm front lip, and two hinged legs that fold flat beside the tray (folded size is about 317 × 20 mm).
- **Bed features:** wide slip-on foot boots (56 × 52 mm) so the legs don't sink into bedding, and recesses under the front edge for adhesive foam so it doesn't dig into a lap.
- The tray prints as **two halves joined by 3 bow-tie keys**, so each half fits a 220 mm printer bed.
- The hinge uses an M4 bolt through a lug on the tray and the leg, and tightening the nut holds the angle by friction.

### What broke / what I changed
- **First version couldn't print flat:** the hinge ears hung below the tray. I moved the hinge to the rear outer corners and made the lugs rise from the flat bottom.
- **Lugs would have hit the laptop's feet:** I trimmed them to 2 mm above the tray surface.
- **Tray too big for a normal bed:** I split it in two and added the bow-tie keys.
- **Leg has no hard stop:** I tried a mechanical stop but it would have stuck up into the laptop area, so I used a friction hinge and wrote this limitation in the README.
- **Foam didn't fit:** the first foam tape I found was 11 mm thick, far too thick for a 1.5 mm recess, so I switched to 1/8" neoprene tape.
- **My first renders had depth-sorting glitches** and hid one leg, so I wrote a simple z-buffer renderer for the README images.

### Checks done
- Both STEP files re-import as valid solids with **no overlapping parts** in the deployed pose, and the legs sweep through the fold without hitting anything.
- BOM is **$50.93 in parts plus about $10 shipping** (PETG filament, M4 hardware pack, foam tape), under the $100 limit.
- Added the README with renders, STL files for each part, and the source scripts.

### Next
- Import the STEP files into Onshape and check that all parts come in correctly.
- Print one tray half first to test the bow-tie pockets and hinge holes, then print the rest.
- Test it with my laptop on a lap and on a mattress, then swap in real photos for the renders.
